{{Short description|Ancient Egyptian unit of volume}}
{{distinguish|Hecate|Heqet}}
{{More footnotes|date=August 2017}}

The '''hekat''' or '''heqat''' (transcribed ''HqA.t'') was an [[ancient Egyptian weights and measures|ancient Egyptian volume unit]] used to measure grain, bread, and beer. 
It equals 4.8&nbsp;[[litre]]s, or about 1.056 [[imperial gallon]]s, in today's measurements.<ref name="alert">{{cite web|url=http://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2012-06/afot-ajh060412.php|title=Ancient jugs hold the secret to practical mathematics in Biblical times|website=EurekAlert!|access-date=2012-06-10|archive-date=2014-10-06|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141006181712/http://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2012-06/afot-ajh060412.php|url-status=dead}} retrieved March 22, 2020 at about 7:00 AM EST.</ref>

==Overview==
Until the [[New Kingdom of Egypt|New Kingdom]] the hekat was one tenth of a khar, later one sixteenth; while the New Kingdom {{Transliteration|egy|oipe}} (transcribed ''ip.t'') contained 4&nbsp;hekat. It was sub-divided into other units &ndash; some for  medical prescriptions &ndash; the   ''hin'' (1/10), ''dja'' (1/64) and ''ro'' (1/320). The ''dja'' was recently evaluated by Tanja Pommerening in 2002 to 1/64 of a hekat (75 cc) in the MK, and 1/64 of an {{Transliteration|egy|oipe}} (1/16 of a hekat, or 300 cc) in the NK, meaning that the ''dja'' was denoted by Horus-Eye imagery. It has been suggested by Pommerening that the NK change came about related to the {{Transliteration|egy|italic=no|oipe}} replacing the hekat as the Pharaonic volume control unit in official lists.

Hana Vymazalova evaluated the hekat unit in 2002 within the [[Akhmim Wooden Tablet]] by showing that five answers were returned to (64/64) when multiplied by the divisors 3, 7, 10, 11 and 13. The [[Rhind Mathematical Papyrus|RMP]] also divided a hekat unity (64/64) by prime and composite numbers ''n'' when 1/64&nbsp;<&nbsp;''n''&nbsp;<&nbsp;64. The binary quotient used [[Eye of Horus#In arithmetic|Eye of Horus]] numbers. The remainder scaled [[Egyptian fraction]]s to 1/320 units named ro. Quotients and unscaled remainders were obtained for the dja, ro and other units when the divisor ''n'' was greater than 64. For example, one the 1/320&nbsp;ro unit was written by Ahmes by solving 320/n&nbsp;ro. Gillings cites 29 examples of two-part statements converted to one-part statements in RMP 82. Ahmes recorded the ''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;3 case by showing (64/64)/3&nbsp;=&nbsp;21/64&nbsp;+&nbsp;1/192 (a modern statement) as written as(16&nbsp;+&nbsp;4&nbsp;+&nbsp;1)/64&nbsp;+&nbsp;5/3&nbsp;×&nbsp;1/320 =&nbsp;1/4&nbsp;+&nbsp;1/16&nbsp;+&nbsp;1/64&nbsp;+&nbsp;1&nbsp;2/3ro (two-part ancient statement). Two-part statements were also converted by Ahmes to an unscaled hin unit by writing&nbsp;3&nbsp;1/3&nbsp;hin.

The hekat measurement unit, and its [[double entry accounting system]], was found beyond the [[Rhind Mathematical Papyrus]]. Another text was the [[Ebers Papyrus]], the best known medical text. The hekat unit was defined, in terms of its volume size, in the [[Moscow Mathematical Papyrus]] by MMP #10, by approximating ''[[pi|π]]'' to around 3.16. The approximation of π was achieved by squaring a circle, increasingly (i.e. for the denominator in terms of {{Transliteration|egy|setats}}: 9, 18, 36, 72, and 81, Gillings, page 141) until the vulgar fraction 256/81 was reached, the only relationship that was used in the Egyptian Middle Kingdom. The MMP scribe found the surface area of a basket equal to: (8d/9)<sup>2</sup> =&nbsp;64d<sup>2</sup>/81, within a cylinder relationship to the hekat. MMP 10 data meant that ''d''&nbsp;=&nbsp;2 defined π for use in hekat volumes as&nbsp;256/81. The 256/81 approximation was also used by [[Ahmes]] and other scribes. The [[ancient Egyptian units of measurement]] discussion further shows that the hekat was 1/30 of a royal cubit<sup>3</sup>, an analysis that needs to double checked, against the ''d''&nbsp;=&nbsp;2 suggestion, which means that ''r''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1, a suggestion that does make sense. One royal cubit of the ancient Egyptian weights and measures =&nbsp;523.5&nbsp;millimeters. ((523.5&nbsp;mm)<sup>3</sup>)&nbsp;/&nbsp;30 =&nbsp;4.78221176&nbsp;liters.

However that may be at least a sphere that has a circumference 523.5 millimeters will actually have a metric volume about 2.42269 liters or roughly half of a hekat or about one sixtieth of a royal cubic cubit to two parts in a hundred.  A modern schoolbook formula has volume=4/3 pi r<sup>3</sup> for example.  In the case of a land where pi=256/81 or about 3.1604938 a similar result can be obtained with the different formula that has been suggested by Zapassky and others where over there the volume of a sphere is given by the quotient of the cube of the circumference divided by six pi<sup>2</sup> (V=c<sup>3</sup>/6π<sup>2</sup>)<ref>Zapassky E, Gadot Y, Finkelstein I, Benenson I (2012) An Ancient Relation between Units of Length and Volume Based on a Sphere. PLoS ONE 7(3): e33895. https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0033895 retrieved March 22, 2020 at about 7:38 AM EST</ref> and in that case the ancient Egyptian volume should come to about 2.386954 liters or about 98.5% of its true volume.
